title: Preferences, Assistive Tools & Inclusive Work Practices
summary: Learn how accessibility preferences, assistive technology, and flexible work practices can help people interact with information and workplace systems more effectively.
objectives: Distinguish ordinary accessibility preferences from institutionally authorized accommodations.
Identify examples of assistive technology and accessible interaction options.
Explain why workers should respect another person's chosen or authorized access method.

vocab.def: A user-controlled choice that changes how information or an interface is presented or experienced.
Technology used to support access, communication, mobility, reading, writing, hearing, vision, or other interactions.
A presentation preference that reduces or removes unnecessary animation and movement.
Another accessible form of the same information, such as plain text, captions, audio, or accessible HTML.

sections.heading: People interact with technology in different ways
sections.body: Some people use screen readers, magnification, captions, alternative input devices, keyboard navigation, speech input, larger text, higher contrast, reduced motion, or other tools and preferences.

sections.heading: A preference does not reveal a diagnosis
sections.body: Choosing larger text, captions, reduced motion, or another accessibility option does not establish why a person uses it and should not be treated as evidence of a medical condition.

sections.heading: Respect the person's access method
sections.body: Do not disable, remove, mock, or override a person's accessibility method because another approach seems easier to you.

sections.heading: Inclusive practices can be ordinary workplace quality
sections.body: Clear agendas, readable documents, flexible communication formats, accessible meeting materials, and predictable instructions can improve work for many people.

practice.prompt: A coworker enables captions during every video meeting. Is it appropriate to assume a diagnosis?
practice.answer: No. An accessibility preference should not be used to infer a disability or diagnosis.

practice.prompt: A worker uses keyboard navigation instead of a mouse. Should a teammate force them to switch methods?
practice.answer: No. If the method is supported and appropriate for the work, their access method should be respected.

quiz.question: What does an accessibility preference tell you about a person's diagnosis?
options: It identifies the exact accommodation they require

lab.objective: Match simulated workplace barriers with possible accessibility features or assistive approaches without diagnosing or labeling any person.

reflectionPrompt: Why is it important to respect how someone accesses information even when their method differs from yours?
